name: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
title: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
answer: XBRL tagging and regulatory filing covers the process of converting financial statements and disclosures into machine-readable XBRL format and submitting them to regulators such as the SEC. It includes mapping line items to standard taxonomies, creating extension elements, validating against filing rules, and managing the review and sign-off workflow. The work spans annual and interim reports, earnings releases, and other structured disclosures. For AI accountants, this is the boundary where human judgment about accounting meaning meets automated tagging and quality checks.

sections.body: XBRL tagging and regulatory filing covers the process of converting financial statements and disclosures into machine-readable XBRL format and submitting them to regulators such as the SEC. It includes mapping line items to standard taxonomies, creating extension elements, validating against filing rules, and managing the review and sign-off workflow. The work spans annual and interim reports, earnings releases, and other structured disclosures. For AI accountants, this is the boundary where human judgment about accounting meaning meets automated tagging and quality checks.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on filing preparation software, taxonomy databases, and validation engines connected to regulator portals. Many teams use cloud-based disclosure management platforms that store company-specific tag selections and link them to source documents. These systems integrate with ERP and consolidation tools to pull figures, and with EDGAR or similar filing systems for submission. Compute is modest by AI standards, but reliable version control and audit trails matter more than speed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Tagging begins with selecting elements from a base taxonomy such as US GAAP or IFRS, then creating company-specific extensions when no standard element fits. Automated tools suggest tags using text similarity, prior filings, and peer mappings, while accountants review and approve each choice. Validation checks cover calculation relationships, dimensional consistency, and regulatory rules before the filing is submitted. The human review remains central because a tag must reflect the economic substance of the line item, not just the label.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on accuracy, liability, and the integrity of the audit trail. A mis-tagged figure can mislead automated analysis and draw regulatory scrutiny, so firms keep detailed logs of who selected, changed, and approved each tag. XBRL filings are public data, but the underlying judgments and internal review notes are not, which creates tension between transparency and confidentiality. Responsibility usually sits with the controller or chief accounting officer, with external auditors providing limited assurance over tagged data in some jurisdictions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automated, continuous, and granular tagging, with regulators expanding structured data requirements beyond financial statements into sustainability and risk disclosures. AI will likely move from suggesting tags to drafting extension definitions and explaining why a peer group mapped a similar item differently. The goal is not to remove accountants but to reduce repetitive mapping work and catch inconsistencies earlier, while keeping human sign-off on the final filing.
